paper_title: AltRA-Test: An Alternative Annotator Test for LLM Judges Without Shared Annotators

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as judges and graders to replace human annotators, raising the question of when such replacement is statistically justified. To support such decisions, the Alternative Annotator Test (Alt-Test) was introduced for dense settings where all items are annotated by the same annotators. However, in many large-scale annotation settings, items are annotated by different subsets of annotators. We therefore propose the Alternative Annotator Test with Resampled Annotations (AltRA-Test), a statistical test that does not require that all items are annotated by the same annotators. AltRA-Test uses a bootstrap that resamples items, draws k human annotations for each item, and substitutes one of them with an LLM annotation. This produces paired all-human and mixed human-LLM panels. A replacement is supported when the inter-annotator agreement (IAA) of the mixed panel is statistically non-inferior to the IAA of the all-human panel, i.e., when the LLM preserves the signal that the human annotators share. We establish that AltRA-Test is a consistent test of asymptotic level alpha. We then evaluate it through simulations and real-world experiments in which we test 18 LLMs and 5 prompting techniques on 20 datasets across text, image, audio, and video. Across these evaluations, about 100 items often suffice for the test. In simulations, where we know whether the LLM is a better or a worse annotator than the humans, AltRA-Test makes more correct replacement decisions than existing baselines. In real-world data experiments, LLMs pass the test in about half of the setups, depending mainly on the task. Since replacement is not always justified, we encourage researchers to test it for their task.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Creating labeled datasets has long depended on human annotation, one of the slowest and most expensive stages of the AI pipeline (Ding et al., 2023; Tan et al., 2024). Researchers use human annotations to train models and to evaluate them, and they draw empirical conclusions from both (Mei et al., 2026; Omar et al., 2026b), so annotation quality directly affects the validity of the resulting models and findings. Large language models (LLMs) offer an appealing alternative: they can annotate quickly, cheaply, and at scale that is difficult to achieve with experts or even with crowd workers (Chiang & Lee, 2023; Gilardi et al., 2023; Tornberg, 2023; Nahum et al., 2025). Indeed, LLMs are increasingly used as annotators, judges (LLM-as-a-judge), and raters (Zheng et al., 2023; Wei et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025; Wu, 2025; Mei et al., 2026). In many AI applications, such as response quality evaluation, there is no ground truth to check labels against (unlike, e.g., checking whether code runs or math answer is correct), and human judgment defines the correct label (Raykar et al., 2010; Paun et al., 2018). Human annotations can serve two different goals. In most cases, they are used to train, evaluate, or judge models. This requires one target per item, so what matters is the signal that the annotators share, and not the variation between individual annotators. In other studies, the disagreement is itself the object of study, and the goal is to capture the different perspectives of the annotators (Aroyo & Welty, 2015; Basile et al., 2021; Uma et al., 2021; Plank, 2022). In this paper, we focus on the first goal, although 1 Figure 1: An illustration of the ALTRA-TEST. The two left boxes present the paired-bootstrap procedure: for each of iterations, we sample items and = 3 annotations per item, replace one annotation with the LLM annotation, and compute IAA for the human-only and humanLLM panels. The substitution gap (b) and adaptive margin ε(b) are then computed. The two right boxes present the decision stage, based on non-inferiority test. Here, qα is the α-quantile statistic; if it is positive, we conclude that the LLM is good alternative to human annotator. we also propose adaptations of our test for the second. Replacing human annotators with LLMs is therefore useful only if the replacement preserves this shared signal (Egami et al., 2023; Gligoric et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025). However, it is not guaranteed that LLMs preserve it. They have been shown to disagree with experts even when their responses appear fluent or confident (Zhou et al., 2024; Griot et al., 2025; Szymanski et al., 2025; Tseng et al., 2025; Wu & Aji, 2025; Omar et al., 2026a), and to systematically diverge from annotators in subjective tasks (Lissak et al., 2024; Elangovan et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025). Accordingly, using an LLM as an alternative to humans requires statistical justification for the replacement (Bavaresco et al., 2025; Calderon et al., 2025b). Since there is no ground truth to compare with, researchers assess human annotation quality using inter-annotator agreement (IAA) (Hayes & Krippendorff, 2007; Klie et al., 2024): if independent annotators consistently agree above chance, the task is well-defined, and the labels capture meaningful shared signal rather than random noise (Artstein & Poesio, 2008; Krippendorff, 2011). Even when IAA is modest, as in subjective tasks where some disagreement is inherent (Basile et al., 2021; Davani et al., 2022; Plank, 2022; Sap et al., 2022; Fleisig et al., 2023), agreement clearly above chance still indicates shared, if noisy, signal. LLM annotations are typically evaluated using accuracy, F1, or correlation with majority-vote label (Ziems et al., 2024; Bavaresco et al., 2025; Elangovan et al., 2025; Guerdan et al., 2025). However, since some disagreement is inherent, individual human annotators also disagree with the majority-vote label, so even human would not score perfectly on these metrics. Their ceiling depends on the task, and without knowing it, it is unclear whether given score is good or poor. As result, such measures cannot provide statistically grounded replacement decision. replacement test should therefore mirror how we evaluate human annotation quality, and test whether the LLM keeps the IAA over all human annotations statistically non-inferior to that of the humans. Two recent works formulate human replacement by LLMs as statistical procedure, the Alternative Annotator Test (ALT-TEST; Calderon et al. (2025b)) and the Statistical Turing Test (STT; He et al. (2025a)). Both assume representative set of items, which we call the evaluation set, each labeled by multiple human annotators. Crucially, they also require the same group of annotators to label every item in this set. However, this requirement is restrictive, and in many common annotation settings it does not hold. In crowdsourcing, workers sometimes choose their assignments and may stop after few items. In preference annotation, large pool of participants contributes only few judgments each, and in demanding tasks, such as verifying the factuality of long document, an annotator can complete only few items. Finally, many existing datasets omit the identities of the annotators (Siththaranjan et al., 2024). In all of these settings, researchers observe multiple human 2 labels for each item, but the items are not all labeled by the same annotators, making existing tests inapplicable. Indeed, 11 of our 20 datasets do not satisfy their requirements. In this work, we introduce the Alternative annotator test with Resampled Annotations (ALTRATEST1; Figure 1), which does not require that the same annotators label all the items in the evaluation set. The test uses paired percentile bootstrap: in each bootstrap sample, it resamples items with replacement, draws human annotations per item, and constructs mixed panel by replacing one human annotation with the LLM annotation. Unlike existing tests, it resamples the annotations within each item, and therefore never uses the identities of the annotators. It then tests whether the mixed-panel IAA is non-inferior to the human-only IAA. An adaptive margin permits small IAA loss proportional to the observed human disagreement, so the same test applies to objective tasks, in which annotators agree strongly, and to subjective tasks, in which some disagreement is inherent. E.g., our calibrated default of = 0.1 allows at most 10% increase in disagreement. We say that an LLM passes the test when we reject the null hypothesis that the mixed-panel IAA is inferior. We theoretically establish that ALTRA-TEST is consistent test of asymptotic level α, i.e., as the number of items grows, it accepts valid replacements with probability approaching 1 and falsely accepts invalid ones with probability at most α. We then use simulations, in which items have latent gold label that annotators observe with noise, and we control whether the LLM is more or less noisy than the humans. This enables us to evaluate the replacement question directly, as we measure each procedures better-model pass rate and worse-model pass rate (i.e., correctly accepting simulated LLMs that are less noisy than simulated humans versus falsely accepting noisier ones). In the setup that the existing tests require, in which the same annotators label all items, ALTRA-TEST dominates ALT-TEST and STT, with higher better-model pass rate at any given worse-model pass rate. We also evaluate the ALTRA-TEST in the setup that motivates it, in which the items are not all labeled by the same annotators, and there, its pass rates remain the same. The simulations also calibrate the default margin constant to = 0.1 and show reliable behavior with around 100 items. In addition, we evaluate the ALTRA-TEST on 20 real-world datasets across text, image, audio, and video, spanning objective and subjective tasks with wide range of human IAA levels. We test 18 LLM judges and 5 prompting techniques. Under the default CoT setting, LLMs pass the test in 71 of 201 judgedataset pairs (35.3%); when each judge uses its best prompting technique, this increases to 95 of 201 (47.3%). We find that replacement is strongly dataset-dependent, and in many passing cases the LLM not only passes the test but increases IAA. Consistent with the simulations, sample-size analyses show that around 100 items often suffice for LLMs that pass with 300 items. We encourage researchers to apply the ALTRA-TEST before delegating annotation to an LLM. As the test examines whether the LLM preserves the signal that the annotators share, its result is meaningful only when this signal exists, and we recommend applying it when human agreement is at least fair (IAA 0.2). We hope it supports more explicit and statistically justified decisions.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: IAA as proxy for human annotation quality. When ground-truth labels are unavailable, researchers commonly assess annotation quality through IAA (Artstein & Poesio, 2008; Krippendorff, 2011). In this work, we use Krippendorffs α, standard chance-corrected IAA coefficient that supports multiple annotators, missing annotations, and nominal or ordinal labels (Hayes & Krippendorff, 2007; Krippendorff, 2011). IAA scores should be interpreted relative to the task: objective or well-specified tasks are expected to yield high agreement, while difficult, ambiguous, or preferencebased tasks may yield lower but still meaningful agreement (Pavlick & Kwiatkowski, 2019; Plank, 2022; Lissak et al., 2024). This interpretation depends on the purpose of annotation. When disagreement is itself the object of study (Aroyo & Welty, 2015; Basile et al., 2021; Uma et al., 2021; Plank, 2022), forcing high IAA may remove the variation that the study aims to measure. Our focus is different (see Section 1), and for such studies we propose variants of our test (see Section 3.2). Even in subjective tasks, such as response-preference annotation, where human IAA may have an inherent ceiling, positive and non-negligible IAA (e.g., 0.2 or higher) indicates that the annotations carry shared signal that an LLM replacement should reflect. We test whether LLMs preserve it. 1 naghamo/altra-test 3 Testing whether LLMs can replace human annotators. Various methods propose correcting or calibrating model-generated labels (Angelopoulos et al., 2023; Lee et al., 2025; Feng et al., 2026), but they do not decide whether replacement is justified. Two recent procedures address replacement as statistical decision. ALT-TEST (Calderon et al., 2025b) holds out each annotator in turn and tests whether an LLM is non-inferior to that annotator in its agreement with the remaining annotators. STT (He et al., 2025a) tests whether human and mixed humanLLM panels are statistically equivalent. Both require the same annotators to label all the items, requirement that often does not hold (see Section 1). ALTRA-TEST removes this requirement. Like ALT-TEST and unlike STT, it answers non-inferiority question. This fits the replacement decision, since LLM annotations are much cheaper than human ones, and researchers may prefer an LLM even at the cost of small loss. An equivalence test does not accept an LLM that increases IAA, even if it captures the shared signal more reliably than typical annotator. Like STT, it uses bootstrap resampling, but unlike both, it does not replace all annotations of single annotator. Instead, for each sampled item, it draws human annotations, replaces one with the LLM annotation, and bases the decision on percentilebootstrap statistic. Its margin also differs. ALT-TEST uses fixed margin that is chosen according to the type of the annotators, and STT derives its margin from the agreement gap between two groups of humans, while the margin of ALTRA-TEST adapts to the observed human disagreement. When all three tests can be applied, ALTRA-TEST dominates both (see Section 4).

sections.title: 3.2 VARIANTS FOR ANNOTATOR PERSPECTIVES
sections.content: The ALTRA-TEST examines whether the LLM preserves the signal that the annotators share, which is our main focus (see Section 1). When the goal is instead to represent the different perspectives of the annotators, the test is not sufficient, since the replaced annotation is drawn from the whole pool, and an LLM can pass while it is not aligned with smaller group of annotators (see Section 4.4). For this goal, we propose two variants of the test. Group-wise testing. When each annotation carries group label, such as demographic attribute, and the LLM should align with each group, the test can be run separately within each group, with panels drawn only from that groups annotations. This requires at least annotations per item in each tested group. Researchers can then require the LLM to pass in every group or in specific groups. Equivalence. Without group labels, stricter criterion can be used. An LLM that makes the annotations more consistent than those of the humans is as undesirable as one that makes them less consistent, as it hides the variation among annotators. The equivalence variant, EQ-ALTRA-TEST, therefore tests whether the substitution gap is within the margin in both directions, and the LLM passes only if it does not increase agreement by more than the margin (see Appendix B.1).

sections.title: 4 SIMULATION-BASED ANALYSIS
sections.content: Simulation studies of statistical tests typically estimate Type error and power under the null and alternative hypotheses of the test. For the ALTRA-TEST, these hypotheses are defined by IAA scores, which are only proxy for the replacement question, since they do not measure whether the LLM is closer than human annotator to the ground-truth label. In this section, we go beyond this proxy and answer the replacement question directly. We generate the ground-truth label of each item and control the noise of the humans and of the LLM. We define the better-model pass rate and the worse-model pass rate, where better model is simulated LLM that is less noisy than the simulated humans and worse model is one that is noisier. good test should accept better models, and worse models should fail it. These measures resemble power and Type error, but they are defined by ground-truth accuracy, which also gives common criterion for comparing tests with different hypotheses. 6 We design the simulations in three stages. We start with basic setup, in which every item has one ground-truth label, all annotators make the same kind of errors, and every annotator labels every item. This setup satisfies the requirements of the existing tests, so we use it to compare the ALTRA-TEST with them and to calibrate its margin (see Section 4.2). We then relax each of these assumptions and vary the parameters of the test and of the task, to examine whether the results still hold (see Section 4.3). Finally, we examine what passing the test means in two cases in which ground-truth label is less meaningful, when annotators form groups with different perspectives and when human agreement is very low (see Section 4.4).

sections.content: Data generation. We simulate annotation tasks with known ground-truth label for each item. For each simulated dataset, we first generate the true item labels and then generate human and LLM annotations by adding noise. The human annotators share noise level, ηh, and the LLM has its own noise level, ηf . Lower noise means higher probability of providing the ground-truth label, so ηf < ηh defines better-model case and ηf > ηh defines worse-model case. Note that nothing in this simulation is specific to humans or LLMs, as we simulate pool of annotators, which we call the humans, and single candidate annotator, which we call the LLM. We compare the ALTRA-TEST with the two known statistical procedures closest to the replacement question. Both procedures require the same annotators to annotate all items. The first baseline is the ALT-TEST (Calderon et al., 2025b). It uses leave-one-annotator-out procedure: each annotator is held out in turn, and statistical test compares whether the LLM is non-inferior, up to margin ε, to the held-out annotator in its alignment with the remaining annotators. The second procedure is STT (He et al., 2025a), which uses bootstrap over items. It first computes the IAA of the all-human panel. Then, for each annotator, it replaces all their annotations with the LLM ones and computes the mean IAA of the resulting mixed panels. It uses Two One-Sided Tests (TOST; Rogers et al., 1993) to test whether the all-human and mixed-panel IAAs are equivalent, i.e., within margin defined by frac parameter. We evaluate STT-Alt, non-inferiority adaptation of STT that uses only the lower one-sided test and for completeness, we also compare the EQ-ALTRA-TEST (see Section 3.2) with the original STT. sections.title: 4.4 ANNOTATOR PERSPECTIVES AND LOW HUMAN AGREEMENT
sections.content: Finally, we examine two cases in which the result of the test should be interpreted with care. The full results are in Appendices B.2 and D.3. Annotators with different perspectives. In subjective tasks, annotators may form groups that hold different perspectives. We simulate two such groups, larger one and smaller one, each with its own ground-truth label for every item, and an LLM that follows the larger group, the smaller group, or mixture of them (see Appendix B.2). As shown in Figure 3, the test behaves as expected when the goal is to preserve the shared signal. An LLM that follows the larger group passes at high rates. In contrast, an LLM that follows the smaller group rarely passes when the larger group dominates the pool. When researchers want the LLM to represent each perspective, we recommend using the variants of the test (see Section 3.2). Low human agreement. Since the margin increases with human disagreement, an uninformative LLM may pass when human agreement is very low. We find that random LLM never passes when the human IAA is above 0.1, and starts to pass below this level (see Appendix D.3). We therefore recommend applying the test only when the human IAA is at least 0.2.

sections.title: 5.1 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
sections.content: We evaluate the ALTRA-TEST on 20 datasets spanning text (12), image (5), audio (2), and video (1). The datasets cover nominal and ordinal tasks with two to ten labels, at least three annotations per item, and human agreement ranging from Rh = 0.01 to 0.90. We use subset of 300 items per dataset and use only items with at least three human labels. Table 5 describes all 20 datasets. We evaluate 18 LLMs as candidate annotators, assigning to each modality the models that natively accept its input: Qwen3-8B (Q3-8b) and Qwen3-14B (Q3-14b), Llama-3.2-3B (L3.2-3b) and Llama-3.1-8B (L3.1-8b), and Gemma-3-4B (G3-4b) and Gemma-3-12B (G3-12b) for text; the visionlanguage models Qwen2.5-VL-3B (Q2.5V-3b) and Qwen2.5-VL-7B (Q2.5V-7b), Llama-3.211B-Vision (L3.2V-11b) and the two Gemma-3 models for image, with the Qwen2.5-VL pair also handling video through sampled frames; and Qwen2.5-Omni-3B (Q2.5-O-3b) and Qwen2-Audio7B (Q2-A-7b) for audio. Alongside these 11 open-weight models, spanning roughly 3B to 14B parameters, we evaluate seven proprietary judges: Gemini-3.1 Pro (Gem-P), Gemini-3.7 Flash (GemF) and Gemini-3.5 Flash-Lite (Gem-L) on all four modalities; GPT-5.6 Terra (GPT-T) and GPT-5.6 Luna (GPT-L) on text and image; and GPT-Audio-1.5 (GPT-A) and GPT-Audio-Mini (GPT-A-M) on audio. This gives 11 text, 10 image, 7 audio and 5 video judges. Dataset details, references and links for all models are provided in Appendix A.3. Each judge is evaluated using up to five prompting techniques (Mizrahi et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025): zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought (Wei et al., 2022), an ensemble of these three (Nahum et al., 2025), and GEPA prompt optimization (Agrawal et al., 2025). GEPA is applied only to open-weight models because of its computational cost. We run the ALTRA-TEST using panels of = 3 annotations (with kc = 3), Krippendorffs α as the agreement coefficient, = 300 bootstrap iterations, significance level of α = 0.05, and the simulation-calibrated margin constant = 0.1. Since real-world data have no gold labels with which can be chosen, we use the value calibrated in the simulations and do not vary it.

sections.title: 5.3 ANNOTATOR PERSPECTIVES IN REAL DATA
sections.content: In Section 4.4, we show with simulations that passing the test means that the LLM preserves the signal that the pool of annotators shares, and that an LLM can pass while it is not aligned with smaller group of annotators. However, when researchers want the LLM to represent the perspectives of different groups of annotators, and not only the shared signal, passing the test with the whole pool is not sufficient. For such cases, we propose two variants of the test (see Section 3.2). In groupwise testing, the test is applied separately within each group, and in the equivalence variant, an LLM that increases the agreement also fails. We next apply group-wise testing to real-world data, and examine whether LLMs that pass the test are also aligned with each group of annotators. We evaluate the equivalence variant with simulations in Appendix B.4. We use DICES-350, conversational-safety dataset in which the demographics of the annotators define 13 groups, by age, education, gender, and race. When panels are drawn from the whole pool and every LLM uses its best prompting technique, four LLMs pass the test, Gemma-3-12B, Gemini3.1-Pro, GPT-5.6-Terra, and GPT-5.6-Luna. When we require an LLM to pass in every group, only 11 Gemma-3-12B passes, and the other three fail in the Latinx group (see Appendix B.3). Group-wise testing therefore exposes misalignment with specific group, which pooled testing averages out.

sections.title: 6 CONCLUSION
sections.content: As LLMs are increasingly used in place of human annotators, their efficiency must be accompanied by statistical evidence that the replacement preserves annotation quality. We propose ALTRATEST, the Alternative Annotator Test with Resampled Annotations, which formulates this as noninferiority test: it asks whether the inter-annotator agreement (IAA) of mixed human-LLM panel is statistically non-inferior to that of an all-human panel. Unlike prior replacement tests, ALTRATEST can be applied to sparse annotation settings, where different items are labeled by different subsets of annotators and no shared panel is required. In simulations, ALTRA-TEST achieves stronger trade-off than existing procedures: for the same rate of false replacements, it accepts more valid ones. Around 100 annotated items often suffice for the test. Replacement is possible in many settings, but the outcome depends more on the dataset than on the judge or prompting technique. The main implication is that LLM annotators should be validated per task rather than adopted as general practice. Because the test is relative to the observed human pool, its verdict should always be reported alongside human IAA: when human agreement is itself very low, passing result does not show that the labels contain useful signal. For the same reason, the test cannot detect errors that the LLM shares with the human annotators. In addition, passing the test means that the LLM preserves the signal that the annotators share, and when the goal is to represent the perspectives of different groups of annotators, the group-wise and equivalence variants of the test should be used. Finally, in this paper, the LLM provides single annotation for each item. We leave for future work an extension of the test that considers the distribution of the LLM annotations for each item, and examines whether it is aligned with the distribution of the human annotations. Such an extension is also suitable for the goal of representing the perspectives of the annotators. We hope ALTRA-TEST helps researchers make more rigorous and transparent decisions about when LLMs can replace human annotators.

sections.title: B ANNOTATOR PERSPECTIVES
sections.content: The ALTRA-TEST asks whether an LLM preserves the signal that the annotators share. This is the relevant question when human labels are used to train, evaluate, or judge models. In these uses, model is trained toward, or scored against, one target per item, so what matters is the judgment on which the annotators converge. In some studies, however, annotators hold distinct perspectives, for example across demographic groups, and the study aims to preserve these perspectives (Aroyo & Welty, 2015; Basile et al., 2021; Uma et al., 2021; Plank, 2022). The standard test is not designed for this second goal, for two reasons. First, the replaced annotation is drawn from the whole pool of an items annotations. The test therefore measures the agreement of the pooled annotations, to which larger group contributes more annotations than smaller one. Second, the test is one-sided, so it accepts an LLM that raises agreement, although such an LLM may remove the variation that the study aims to capture. In this section, we address both points. In Appendix B.1, we start by defining two variants of the test, groupwise testing and an equivalence test. Then, in Appendix B.2, we use simulations with groups of annotators to show how the standard test behaves when perspectives differ. In Appendix B.3, we apply group-wise testing to real dataset, and finally, in Appendix B.4, we evaluate the equivalence variant in simulation. We leave for future work an extension of the test that considers the distribution of the LLM annotations for each item, and examines whether it is aligned with the distribution of the human annotations. B.1 VARIANTS OF THE TEST Group-wise testing. Suppose that every annotation carries group label, such as demographic attribute of its annotator. For group g, let Hi denote the annotations of item xi that come from this group. The group-wise test applies the ALTRA-TEST without any change to the items with at least such annotations, and it draws the panels only from . The human-only agreement, the margin, and the decision statistic are then all computed within the group, so the test compares the LLM with typical annotator of that group. Researchers can require the LLM to pass in every group, or only in the groups of interest. Since this involves several tests, researchers should account for multiple comparisons when drawing conclusions about individual groups. In addition, the chance that an LLM passes in every group decreases as the number of groups grows. Each tested group also needs enough items with at least annotations from that group. In Section 4, we show that about 100 items are enough for high better-model pass rate. Equivalence. The ALTRA-TEST is non-inferiority test, so an LLM that increases the agreement of the panel passes it. In some settings, we instead want to test whether the LLM is indistinguishable from human annotator. This is the case when the annotations should reflect human judgment and its variation, since labels that are more consistent than the human ones misrepresent the annotators. In such settings, an LLM that increases agreement by more than the margin should fail the test, like an LLM that decreases it. We therefore define the EQ-ALTRA-TEST, which tests whether the substitution gap is within the margin in both directions: The test uses the same bootstrap iterations as the ALTRA-TEST, and the LLM passes when H0 : ε vs. H1 : < ε. α > 0 and 1α < 0, (1) (2) 1α is the (1 where ε(b). The first condition is the non-inferiority test of Section 3.1. The second condition tests that the mixed-panel agreement does not exceed the human-only agreement by more than the margin. Together, they form the Two One-Sided Tests procedure (TOST; Rogers et al., 1993), applied to bootstrap quantiles. α)-quantile of (b) (cid:98) Two points should be noted when using the EQ-ALTRA-TEST. First, the constant must be recalibrated. We calibrated = 0.1 for the non-inferiority test, and with the second condition, this value reduces the better-model pass rate from 0.984 to 0.030 (see Appendix B.4). Researchers should choose according to the tolerance that their setting requires; in Appendix B.4, we use = 0.125. Second, failure has different meaning. We cannot conclude that the LLM is worse than the humans, only that it is distinguishable from them, possibly because it is better. 25 B.2 SIMULATIONS WITH ANNOTATOR GROUPS Setup. We simulate task in which the annotators form two groups with different perspectives, larger group and smaller group. Each group has its own label prior and its own gold label for every item, and the annotators of group are noisy around the gold label of their group, as in Section 4. We vary the sizes of the two groups from 9+1 to 5+5 annotators. The simulated LLM follows one of four profiles. It labels like an annotator of the larger group, like an annotator of the smaller group, like an equal mixture of the two, or like mixture in proportion to the group sizes. Since no profile is correct by construction, we report the pass rate of each profile, with = 0.1 and = 200. We also repeat the simulation when every human annotator Dirichlet(1L) and errs according to (πg + bj)/2, where πg is the label prior of the has personal bias bj annotators group. The test behaves as expected for shared signal. Figure 3 presents the results. When annotators form groups, the signal that the pool shares is mainly the judgment of the larger group. Accordingly, an LLM that follows the larger group passes the test at high rates, while an LLM that follows the smaller group rarely passes when the larger group dominates the pool, even when it is less noisy than the humans. Such an LLM disagrees with most of the annotators, so replacing human annotation with its annotation reduces the agreement of the pool. As the two groups approach equal size, neither group dominates the pool, and the gap between the profiles closes. The two mixtures lead to the same conclusion. An LLM that mixes the groups in proportion to their sizes behaves like an annotator drawn at random from the pool, and its pass rates are close to those of the LLM that follows the larger group. The equal mixture represents the smaller group more than the pool does, and it passes less often when the groups are unequal. For every profile, the pass rate decreases as the LLM becomes noisier, so the test remains sensitive to the quality of the LLM. However, noise alone does not determine the result. An LLM that follows the larger group can pass even when it is somewhat noisier than the humans, since it agrees with most annotators more than randomly drawn annotator does. Finally, the results with and without personal bias are nearly identical. When perspectives should be represented. The same behavior is not desired when the goal is to represent each perspective. In this simulation, an LLM that follows the smaller group faithfully rarely passes, and an LLM that ignores the smaller group passes. For this goal, we therefore recommend the variants of Appendix B.1. In Appendix B.3, we apply group-wise testing to real dataset, and in Appendix B.4, we evaluate the equivalence variant in simulation. B.3 GROUP-WISE TESTING ON DICES-350 DICES-350 reports the demographics of its annotators. We use them to define 13 groups, according to age, education, gender, and race  (Table 6)  . Every annotator labels every item, so each group has between 7 and 75 annotations per item. The human agreement is similar in all groups, between 0.14 and 0.25, compared with 0.20 for the whole pool. Every LLM uses its best prompting technique. When panels are drawn from the whole pool, four LLMs pass the ALTRA-TEST. When panels are drawn within each group and an LLM must pass in all 13 groups, only G3-12b passes. Gem-P and GPT-T fail only in the Latinx group, and GPT-L fails in three groups, including the Latinx group. In all these cases, the decision statistic is only slightly below zero. Group-wise testing therefore exposes misalignment with one group, which pooled testing averages out. The choice between the two depends on whether the goal is to match the pooled signal or to represent each group. Selecting panels with diverse labels cannot replace group labels, because label diversity alone does not distinguish minority perspective from annotation noise. We first replace only the decision rule of the ALTRA-TEST with the equivalence rule of Appendix B.1 and keep everything else fixed. At = 0.1, the better-model pass rate drops from 0.984 to 0.030.
